Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Sūrat al-Ra'd (Surah of Thunder)

Tafsir of Sūrat al-Ra'd. It is Meccan, except for two verses: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be struck by a calamity for what they have done﴾, and the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger"﴾ to the end of the verse, for these two are Medinan.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra﴾. They said: its meaning is "I am Allah, the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing." It was also said: the alif is from Allah, the lam is from Jibril (Gabriel), the mim is from Muhammad, and the ra' is from the sending (irsal) of Allah to him, meaning Muhammad. We have already explained other than this before.

And His saying: ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ has been explained in Sūrat Yūsuf. And His saying: ﴿And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth﴾. The revelation (inzal) is the conveying from above to below. The meaning of the verse is that what Allah sent down to you through Jibril is the truth, and the truth is the opposite of falsehood. It was also said: it is placing a thing in its proper place as wisdom requires. And His saying: ﴿But most of the people do not believe﴾ means among the Jews, the Christians, and the polytheists.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 2:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿It is Allah who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see.﴾ The "amad" (pillars, sing. 'amud) is an elongated body that prevents what is raised from leaning. Regarding the meaning of His words ﴿without pillars﴾ there are two opinions. The first, and it is the more sound, is that its meaning is: He raised the heavens without pillars ﴿that you see﴾ as such.

The people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) have said: If the heavens had pillars, we would see them, because the pillars of a thick body are made of a thick body, so they must be visible. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah and most of the exegetes.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The meaning of the verse is: He raised the heavens without pillars that you see.

His words ﴿that you see﴾ refer back to the pillars, as if he said: they have pillars that you do not see. Some claimed that they have pillars upon Mount Qaf, that the sky is above them like a dome, and that Mount Qaf encircles the world and is made of green emerald. The correct view is what we have explained.

His words ﴿Then He istawa (established Himself) upon the Throne﴾: we have already explained the meaning. His words ﴿and subjected the sun and the moon﴾ mean: He made the sun and the moon subservient, so they are subjugated and compelled, running according to what Allah wills. His words ﴿each runs to a term appointed﴾ mean: for a set period of time. His words ﴿He arranges the affair﴾: arrangement (tadbir) from Allah the Exalted is His doing things in accordance with what wisdom requires. His words ﴿He details the signs﴾ mean He makes the proofs clear. His words ﴿so that you may be certain of the meeting with your Lord﴾ mean: that you may believe.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 3:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth﴾, the verse. The earth was originally a rounded lump of clay (madarah mudawwarah), and Allah the Exalted spread it out and stretched it.

His words: ﴿and placed therein firmly set mountains﴾, meaning: firm mountains (jibalan thawabit).

His words: ﴿and rivers﴾. The anhar (rivers) are the wide channels of water (majari al-ma', sing. majra).

His words: ﴿and of all the fruits He placed therein two mates, two﴾, meaning: two kinds, two: red and yellow, sweet and sour. It has also been said that His words ﴿two﴾ are an emphasis of His words ﴿two mates﴾.

His words: ﴿He causes the night to cover the day﴾, its meaning: He clothes the day with the darkness of the night, and clothes the darkness of the night with the light of the day. His words: ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, meaning: proofs, ﴿for a people who reflect﴾. Tafakkur (reflection) is the turning of the heart in seeking the meanings of things.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 4:

Regarding the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And in the earth are neighbouring tracts﴾, there are two opinions.

The first: that there is an elision (hadhf) in it. It is as if He said: "And in the earth are neighbouring tracts and non-neighbouring tracts." This is like the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And garments that protect you from the heat﴾, meaning: garments that protect you from the heat and the cold.

The second opinion: that there is no elision in the verse, and its meaning is sound. Regarding "neighbouring" (mutajawirat) there are two views. The first: that its meaning is that they are adjacent in appearance but differ in meaning. This one is saline and this one is sweet; this one yields little and this one yields much; this one is cultivated (mazra'a) and this one is planted with trees (maghrasa); and this one is neither cultivated nor planted.

The second view: its meaning is: this one is inhabited (amira), and this one is uninhabited (ghamira); this one is deserts and wastelands, and this one is mountains and valleys. Accordingly, when we supply in the verse "neighbouring and non-neighbouring," the neighbouring tracts are the inhabited lands that are joined to one another, and the non-neighbouring tracts are the ruined lands in which are valleys and sand dunes (dakadik).

As for His words: ﴿and gardens of grapevines﴾, meaning: orchards of grapevines. His words: ﴿and tilth and palm trees﴾ are of known meaning. His words: ﴿clustered and non-clustered palms﴾: it has been read as "sinwan" with a damma (ṣunwān), while the well-known reading is "ṣinwān" with a kasra. In the transmitted reports traced back (al-athar al-musnada) from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The ṣinwān is the palm clustered together, and the non-ṣinwān is the scattered one." The well-known usage in the language is that ṣinwān are palm trees with a single root, and non-ṣinwān is a single palm tree with its own root.

As for His words: ﴿watered with one water﴾: water (al-ma') is a thin, fluid body that is drunk, by which every growing thing lives. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾. In the verse there is a refutation of the naturalists (aṣḥāb al-ṭabī'a), for water is one, air is one, earth is one, and heat is one, while the fruits differ in colour and taste, and in yield, few or abundant. Nature is one, and it is impossible that it should produce two different things; this shows that all of it is from Allah, the Exalted.

In the Jami' of Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi, on the authority of Abu Hurayra, regarding the Prophet's words (ﷺ) concerning ﴿and We favour some of them over others in food﴾, he said: "This is sweet and this is sour, and this is a dagal (a type of date) and this is a Persian (date)."

As for His words: ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, meaning: proofs, ﴿for a people who reason﴾, meaning: who understand. They recited verses concerning the ṣinwān:

(Knowledge and forbearance are two qualities of nobility; for a man they are an adornment when they are combined.)

(Two that are twins, their beauty is not complete except by combining this and that together.)

It has also been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The paternal uncle of a man is the ṣinw of his father" (ʿamm al-rajul ṣinw abīhi), meaning: he and his father share a single root.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying﴾. Al-ʿajab (amazement): the soul's change upon seeing something deemed unlikely in customary practice. The address is to the Messenger, and its meaning is: you are amazed; so it is amazing that they deny the afterlife resurrection while they affirm that God originated creation. It is firmly established in hearts that restoration is easier than initiation; so this is the locus of amazement. In the proverbs: there is no good in one who is not amazed by what is amazing, and more contemptible than him is one who is amazed by what is not amazing.

And His saying: ﴿When we have become dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ This is the meaning of their denial of resurrection.

And His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord﴾ means they denied their Lord.

And His saying: ﴿And those are the shackles around their necks﴾. The ghull (shackle) is a collar by which the hand is joined to the neck, and these shackles are of fire. And His saying: ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾: its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 6:

The words of the Most High: ﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good.﴾ Al-isti'jal (hastening) is seeking to bring a matter forward before its (appointed) time has come. God, the Most High, had delayed the punishment of total annihilation (al-istiṣlam) from the polytheists out of honour for the Prophet. The "evil" here is the punishment, and the "good" is well-being (al-'afiyah). The meaning is that they seek punishment instead of well-being. This is indicated by the words of the Most High: ﴿And when they said, "O God, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky"﴾ and His words: ﴿A questioner asked about a punishment that will surely fall.﴾

As for His words: ﴿And exemplary punishments (al-mathulat) have already passed before them.﴾ It is narrated from Mujahid that he said: "al-mathulat" means "the examples (al-amthal)." But most (scholars) hold that al-mathulat means "the punishments." Al-A'mash recited it as "al-mathulat" with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the ta', and it is related from him that he recited "al-muthulat" with a damma on the mim and a sukun on the tha'; the meanings are close to one another.

As for His words: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing.﴾ Its meaning: He is one who overlooks the wrongdoing of people. ﴿And indeed, your Lord is severe in punishment.﴾ In some of the chains of narration (al-masanid) it is reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that the Prophet (ﷺ) said when this verse was revealed: "Were it not for God's grace and His overlooking, no one would enjoy life at all; and were it not for His warning and His punishment, every person would rely (on their own deeds)."

"The saying of Him, the Exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, 'Why has a sign not been sent down upon him from his Lord?'﴾ Its meaning: 'Why has a sign not been sent down upon him of the kind we propose,' for in fact signs had already been sent down upon him.

And His saying: ﴿You are only a warner﴾: one who frightens, or one who conveys the revelation with warning.

And His saying: ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾: concerning it there are several opinions. Most of the scholars hold that its meaning is: 'And for every people there is a prophet who calls them to God.' The second opinion: 'And for every people there is a guide,' meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). And it was said: the guide is God."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 8:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Allah knows what every female bears﴾ mean: Allah knows what every female bears, whether male or female, or whether its creation is complete or incomplete, or whether it is one or two or more.

His words: ﴿And what the wombs diminish and what they increase﴾. Al-ghaydh (diminution) is decrease. This is what Mujahid and others said. In some reports it is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When rain is scarce in summer, and the child is diminished, and the noble decline in diminution, and the base overflow in abundance..." — the report continues.

Concerning the diminishing and increasing of the wombs there are three opinions. The first: it is the decrease below seven months and the increase beyond nine months. The second: it is the decrease by miscarriage of an unformed fetus, and the increase by the completion of creation. The third: it is the decrease by menstruation during pregnancy, and the increase by the absence of menstruation during pregnancy; for the child diminishes when the woman sheds blood during pregnancy, and it is completed when she does not shed it. It is related from Makhul that he said: menstrual blood is the nourishment of the child in the womb.

His words: ﴿And everything with Him is by measure﴾, meaning: by decree.
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Great, the Most High﴾. He means: the Most High above what the polytheists say.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whether of you conceals speech or openly declares it﴾ and so on. Its meaning: in the knowledge of God, the one who keeps speech secret and the one who speaks it aloud are equal.

And His saying: ﴿and whoever hides himself by night﴾, i.e., conceals himself in the darkness of the night. And His saying: ﴿and goes forth freely by day﴾, i.e., appears openly and goes about by day. The sarb (path) is the road; the Arabs say: "Leave him his sarb," meaning his path. Some scholars of the ma'ani (meanings of the Qur'an) claimed that His saying: ﴿and whoever hides himself by night﴾ means one who is visible by night, as it is said: khafiya (to be hidden) when it appeared, and akhfa (to conceal) when it concealed. The poet said:

(They appeared from their openings as if the rain of a layered cloud had revealed them.)

And His saying: ﴿and goes forth freely by day﴾ means one who is hidden (mustakinn) by day, as it is said: asraba al-wahsh (the wild beasts took cover) when they hid. The first opinion is the most correct.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 11:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For him are successive angels before him and behind him⦆ — the verse. There are several opinions regarding this verse, the most apparent of which is that the mu'aqqibat (successive ones) are the angels, and the mu'aqqibat are those that follow one another, meaning that some of them depart and others come after them. It has been authentically related through the narration of Abu Hurairah from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, Allah has angels who succeed one another among you, and they gather at the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer. Then those who spent the night among you ascend, and Allah asks them, although He knows best: 'How did you leave My servants?' They say: 'We came to them while they were praying, and we left them while they were praying.'"

The second opinion is what has been related from Ikrimah, who said: the verse refers to the rulers and their guards.

The third opinion is what has been related from Ibn Jurayj, who said: the verse refers to the one who sits on the right and the left, recording, and this is in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When the two receivers receive, one seated on the right and one on the left⦆ [50:17].

As for His saying: ﴿They guard him by the command of Allah⦆, the majority hold that His saying ﴿by the command of Allah⦆ means that they guard him by the permission of Allah; so when the decree comes, they leave him between it and himself. In some reports it is said that Allah entrusts angels with the sleeper, who guard him from the living and from harmful creatures; and if anything intends to harm him, they say: "Behind you, behind you," except for something that is destined to befall him.

Amr ibn Abi Jundub related: We were with Sa'id ibn Qais al-Hamdani when Ali came, leaning on a staff of his. We said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, are you not afraid that someone will assassinate you?" He said: "Indeed, Allah, the Exalted, has entrusted to the son of Adam angels who guard him; so when the decree comes, they leave him between it and himself."

Regarding His saying ﴿by the command of Allah⦆ there is another opinion, namely that it is according to the meaning of inversion and reordering, as if Allah, the Exalted, said: "For him are successive ones of His command who guard him before him and behind him." It was also said: "by the command of Allah" means: by what Allah has commanded of protection for him. It is related from Ibn Abbas that he recited: "For him are successive ones before him and guardians behind him." And it has been read in the irregular (shadh) reading: "For him are mu'aqqibun before him and behind him."

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not change what is with a people⦆, its meaning is: He does not change any blessing that is with a people ﴿until they change what is in themselves⦆ through disobedience.

As for His saying: ﴿And when Allah wills harm for a people⦆, in the verse there is a clear refutation of the Qadariyyah, and its meaning is: affliction and punishment ﴿there is no repelling it⦆, i.e., there is no one who can repel it. ﴿And they have not, besides Him, any protector⦆, i.e., no guardian who would prevent them and give them victory. The poet said:

(There is nothing in the heaven but the All-Merciful as a protector...)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 12:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as a fear and as a hope﴾. Al-Barq (lightning): a bright light, likened to a pillar of fire, from the kindling of the clouds. The well-known explanation transmitted from the early generation (al-salaf) is that the lightning is whips (makhariq) in the hands of the angels, made of fire, with which they drive the clouds wherever God, the Exalted, wills.

As for His words ﴿as a fear and as a hope﴾, there are several opinions. The first: the fear is of the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqah), and the hope is for the benefit of the rain.

The second: the fear is for the traveler, for it is the habit of the traveler to be harmed by the rain, and the hope is for the one who stays at home, for the one who stays at home hopes for fertility through the rain.

﴿...with His praise, and the angels from fear of Him. And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, while they dispute concerning God﴾.

The third: the fear is of rain at the wrong time and in the wrong place, and the hope is when it comes at its proper time and place. Among the lands, [some] when they are rained upon suffer drought, like Egypt and others, and when they are not rained upon they become fertile.

In some reports from the Prophet (ﷺ) it is related that God, the Exalted, says: "If My servants obeyed Me, I would give them rain by night and cause the sun to rise upon them by day, and I would not make them hear the sound of thunder."

As for His words ﴿and He produces the heavy clouds﴾, meaning heavy with water. It is related from ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The cloud is the sieve of the sky." And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "God, the Exalted, created the clouds once every seven years."

And His saying: ﴿And the thunder glorifies Him with His praise﴾. Most of the exegetes (mufassirun) hold that the thunder (al-Ra'd) is an angel, and the sound that is heard from it is its glorification (tasbih). This is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) when the Jews asked him about the thunder, and he mentioned in it that the sound is its driving (zajr) of the clouds. This has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan. And from Qatadah, who said: "This is a servant of Allah, the Exalted, who hears and obeys."

In the traditions (al-athar): when a person hears the thunder, he should say: "Glory be to the One whom it glorifies." This has been narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr and others. And from 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Whoever, when he hears the sound of the thunder, says: 'Glory be to the One whom the thunder glorifies with His praise, and the angels out of fear of Him, and He is Powerful over everything,' then if a thunderbolt strikes him, its blood-money (diyah) is upon [Allah]."

And from Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir, who said: "The thunderbolt strikes the Muslim and the non-Muslim, but it does not strike the one who remembers (Allah)."

There is another opinion regarding the thunder, namely that it is the sound of the collision of the heavenly bodies (ajram 'ulwiyyah). The correct view is the first. It has also been said: the thunder is the speech of the clouds, and the lightning is their laughter.

And His saying ﴿and the angels out of His awe﴾ means: and the angels glorify Him out of His awe. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that Allah, the Exalted, has angels who weep out of fear of Him from the day He created them, angels in bowing (ruku'), angels in prostration (sujud), and angels in glorification (tasbih) whom nothing distracts from that.

And His saying: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts (sawa'iq) and strikes with them whom He wills﴾. The sa'iqah is the destroying punishment, and it descends from the lightning in some circumstances, burning whatever it strikes. The verse was revealed concerning Arbad ibn Rabi'ah, when he came to the Prophet and said: "Of what is your Lord made? Of pearl, or ruby, or gold [or silver]?" Then a thunderbolt descended from the sky and burned him. His brother Labid ibn Rabi'ah lamented him, saying:

(I fear for Arbad the calamities, and I do not dread the rising of al-Simak and al-Asad)

(The lightning and the thunderbolts have bereaved me of the horseman, on the day of the terrible battle, the Najd)

It is said that he came with 'Amir ibn Tufayl, intending to treacherously kill the Prophet, but his hand became stiff upon the hilt of the sword. When he left the presence of the Messenger of Allah, a thunderbolt struck him on a clear, scorching day. As for 'Amir, he was afflicted with a boil (ghuddah), and he died in the house of a woman of the Salul clan, and he kept saying: "A boil like the boil of a camel, and death in the house of a woman of Salul."

It is reported that a Jew came to the Prophet and asked him: "Of what is your Lord made?" Then a thunderbolt descended and burned him.

And His saying: ﴿while they dispute concerning Allah﴾ means: they argue and say about Allah what they have no knowledge of. It was also said: "while they dispute concerning Allah" means: they deny the greatness of Allah.

And His saying: ﴿and He is Mighty in strength (shadid al-mihal)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Mighty in power (shadid al-hawl)," and from this is the saying: "There is no power nor strength except with Allah." It was also said: "Mighty in strength" means severe in retribution. And from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "severe in seizing." It was also said: "severe in destruction." And it was said: "severe in plotting." The poet said:

(A branch of the nabi tree swaying on the bough of glory, generous in bounty, mighty in strength)

And it was recited in the irregular reading (shadhdh): "shadid al-mihal" with a fatḥah on the mīm.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To Him is the call of truth﴾ refers to the testimony that there is no god but Allah. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and others. It was also said: "The call of truth" is calling upon Him with sincerity (ikhlas), and calling with sincerity is only directed to Allah. Do you not see that Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So call upon Allah, being sincere to Him in religion﴾?

His saying: ﴿And those who call upon other than Him﴾, meaning the idols, ﴿do not respond to them with anything﴾, meaning they do not answer them with anything. And His saying: ﴿except like one who extends his hands toward water﴾. There are two opinions regarding this. The first: it is like one who grasps water, and whoever grasps water has nothing left in his hand. The poet said:

(So I have become, regarding what was between me and her, of affection like the one who grasps water in his hand.)

The second opinion, which is the well-known one, is that His saying ﴿like one who extends his hands toward water﴾ means: like the thirsty person who gestures with his palm toward water while there is a distance between him and the water that he cannot reach. He gestures with his palm and calls with his tongue, but does not reach it. Likewise, whoever calls upon the idols for harm or benefit does not attain anything by his supplication. His saying ﴿that it may reach his mouth﴾ means that it may reach his mouth. ﴿But it will not reach it﴾ means it will not reach him.

His saying: ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾, meaning nothing but in mistake and falsehood.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 15:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly﴾. He means: whoever is in the heavens prostrates willingly, and whoever is on the earth, some of them prostrate willingly and some of them unwillingly. Sujud (prostration) is submission with humility, and it was said: the prostration of things is their humbling and their subjugation to what they are intended for and what they are made subservient to. His saying: ﴿and their shadows﴾. They said: the shadow of the disbeliever prostrates unwillingly, and the disbeliever prostrates unwillingly; and the shadow of the believer prostrates willingly, and likewise the believer prostrates willingly. This is the saying transmitted from the early generations (al-salaf). It was said: the prostration of the shadow is its subjugation and humbling to what it is intended for. It was said: the meaning of His saying ﴿and their shadows﴾ is their persons (ashkhas), ﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾, meaning in the early hours and the evenings.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 16:

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?﴾ Its meaning: Say, O Muhammad: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Then He commanded him to answer, and said: ﴿Say: Allah.﴾ It is narrated that he (ﷺ) only said this to the polytheists, who insisted and said: "You answer." So Allah commanded him, and said: ﴿Say: Allah.﴾ This answer was valid with them only because they acknowledged that Allah is their Creator and the Creator of the heavens and the earth.

His statement: ﴿Say: Have you then taken protectors other than Him?﴾ Its meaning: that you, despite your acknowledgment that Allah is your Creator and the Creator of the heavens and the earth, have taken protectors other than Him, meaning: the idols. ﴿They have no power to benefit or harm themselves﴾ meaning: they are powerless. So if they have no power to benefit or harm themselves, how could they have power over you?

His statement: ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾ It is a parable for the believer and the disbeliever, and for faith and disbelief. So He said: (﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾ or are the darknesses and the light equal?) Meaning: just as the blind and the seeing are not equal, nor are the darknesses and the light, so too the believer and the disbeliever, and faith and disbelief, are not equal.

His statement: ﴿Or have they assigned to Allah partners who created as He creates, so that the creation became confusing to them?﴾ Meaning: have they made for Allah partners ﴿who created as He created, so that the creation appeared similar to them﴾, i.e., what they created was confused with what Allah created. The meaning of the verse: just as they recognized that the idols do not create as Allah creates, so they should not be worshipped with the worship due to Allah.

His statement: ﴿Say: Allah is the Creator of all things﴾ its meaning is apparent. His statement ﴿And He is the One, the Irresistible﴾: "The One" (al-Wahid) is that which cannot be divided. It may also be two things that cannot be divided in meaning, and it is called "one," as in their saying: "one dinar," because it cannot be divided in its dinarness. "Al-Qahhar" is the Overpowering, the one whom nothing can overcome. In some reports: "Glory be to Him who is mighty by His power and subdues His servants by death."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He sends down water from the sky﴾. This is a parable that Allah struck in the Qur'an, and He struck the valleys as a parable for the hearts. So His saying ﴿He sends down water from the sky﴾ means rain, ﴿and the valleys flow according to their measure﴾. It was recited as "bi-qadarihā" (according to their measure), recited by Abu al-Ash'hab al-'Uqayli. The meaning is: according to their measure of smallness and greatness. Likewise, hearts carry the Qur'an according to their measure of constriction and expansiveness.

And His saying: ﴿So the torrent carries a foaming scum﴾. Zabad (foam) is the impurity that appears on the surface of water, and likewise on the surface of a cooking pot, and likewise at the mouth of a camel. His saying: ﴿rābiyan﴾ means floating, rising high. Here the first parable is complete. Then he mentioned a second parable, which is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And from that which they heat up in the fire﴾, and "that which you heat in it." Al-Iqad (kindling) is placing fire beneath a thing so that it melts.

His saying: ﴿seeking an ornament﴾ means: seeking ornament. What is heated here is gold and silver, because ornaments are sought from them. His saying: ﴿or utensils﴾ means: or seeking utensils. That is from tin, copper and other things that are heated, and al-matā' (utensils) are the vessels made from these substances.

His saying: ﴿a foam like it﴾, meaning a foam like the foam of water. ﴿Thus Allah strikes the truth and falsehood﴾, meaning: thus Allah makes clear the truth and falsehood through the striking of parables. Then He said: ﴿As for the foam, it passes away as scum﴾, meaning it is lost and vain. It is said: ajfa'a al-qidr (the pot foamed over) when it boils over from its sides, and the foam departs. Abu Zayd al-Lughawi mentioned that Ru'ba ibn al-'Ajjaj recited: "fa-ammā al-zabadu fa-yadhhabu jufālan," and the meaning is close to the first.

His saying: ﴿But as for that which benefits people, it remains in the earth﴾, meaning: water, gold, silver, iron, lead, tin and copper. His saying: ﴿it remains in the earth﴾ means it endures and does not perish.

His saying: ﴿Thus Allah strikes the parables﴾: He made this a parable for truth and falsehood in the hearts, meaning: falsehood is like the foam, which passes away, perishes and is destroyed, while truth is like the water and like these things, which remains and endures in the hearts. Some of them said: this is a consolation for the believers, meaning that the affair of the polytheists is like the foam, which appears in form as something firm while having no reality, and the affair of the believers is like the water that settles in its place, so it has stability and permanence. It is said: falsehood has a rounding (jawlah), and truth has a dominion (dawlah).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 18:

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿For those who respond to their Lord, there is the best (reward)﴾ — the verse — we have already explained that al-istijabah (response) and al-ijabah (answer) have one and the same meaning. As for His statement ﴿al-husna﴾ (the best), most of the scholars say it is Paradise. It has also been said that it is provision and well-being in this world and bliss in the Hereafter. Al-husna is the elative form (af'al) derived from al-husn (goodness).

As for His statement ﴿And those who do not respond to Him﴾, meaning: those who do not answer Him. As for His statement ﴿If they had all that is on the earth entirely, and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom﴾, meaning: they would expend that as a ransom from the Fire.

As for His statement ﴿Those – for them is an evil reckoning﴾, it is narrated from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that he said to Farqad: "O Fariqad, do you know what evil reckoning is? It is that one is called to account for all the sins and nothing of them is forgiven." And it is authentically related from the Prophet (ﷺ), on the narration of ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her): "Whoever is subjected to a thorough reckoning will be punished," and in another narration, "will be destroyed." It has also been said that evil reckoning is that no good deed is accepted and no evil deed is pardoned. As for His statement ﴿And their abode is Hell﴾, meaning: their place of settlement is Hell.

As for His statement ﴿And wretched is the resting-place﴾, meaning: wretched is what they have prepared for themselves, that is, wretched is what has been prepared for them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is he who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind?﴾ The verse was revealed concerning Hamzah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib and Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. The first is Hamzah and the second is Abu Jahl. It is also said: it was revealed concerning ʿAmmar ibn Yasir and Abu Jahl.

And His saying: ﴿Only the people of understanding will be reminded﴾, meaning: the people of understanding (ulu al-albab, "those endowed with intellect") will take heed. The meaning of the verse is that one who sees the truth and follows it, and one who does not see the truth and does not follow it, are never equal.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 20:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah﴾. The meaning is apparent. It has also been said: the covenant of Allah, exalted is He, is what Allah took as a covenant from the offspring of Adam when He took them from his loins.

And His saying: ﴿and do not break the pledge﴾ is a confirmation of the fulfilment mentioned before.

And His saying: ﴿And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾ means: they believe in all the prophets. It was also said: they maintain the ties of kinship and do not sever them.

And His saying: ﴿and fear their Lord﴾, meaning: they are afraid of their Lord. ﴿And they dread the evil reckoning﴾, meaning: they stand in awe of the evil reckoning, and we have already explained the evil reckoning.

And His saying: ﴿Those who are patient, seeking the face of their Lord﴾, meaning: they were patient in obeying God's command [seeking the pleasure of] their Lord. It was also said: they were patient with poverty, misfortunes and trials. It was also said: they were patient in refraining from sins. It was also said: they were patient in restraining themselves from the desires and pleasures of this world.

And His saying: ﴿They repel evil with good﴾, meaning: they repel an evil deed with a good deed. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾, and the meaning of the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "If you commit an evil deed, then do a good deed beside it, and it will erase it." There is another view regarding the verse, that the evil (sayyi'ah) is sin (dhanb) and the good (hasanah) is repentance (tawbah). Its meaning is: they repel sin with repentance. And in a report: "Nothing is more effective against an old sin than a recent repentance."

His saying: ﴿For them is the good end of the abode﴾, i.e., Paradise. Its meaning: for them is the end of the abode of reward.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 23:

His saying: ﴿Gardens of Eden, which they will enter﴾ means: gardens [for abiding].

His saying: ﴿which they will enter﴾, its meaning is well known. His saying: ﴿and whoever is righteous among their forefathers﴾ means: and whoever is righteous among their forefathers will also enter them, ﴿and their spouses and their offspring﴾. There is a report (khabar) that the believer will enter Paradise and see his offspring in it, and he will say: "When did you enter it?" They will say: "We have been waiting for you since long ago." And God knows best.

His saying: ﴿and the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ means: from the gates of Paradise. It was also said: from the gates of the palaces.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 24:

And His words: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ mean: they greet them with peace (salaman). It is also said: they say, "May Allah have saved you from the calamities which you used to fear from them." In the reports it is related that they (i.e., the angels) come with gifts and presents from Allah, Exalted is He, according to the measure of every day of the days of this world, thirteen times.

And His words: ﴿Because you were patient﴾ have already been explained. And His words: ﴿How excellent is the final abode﴾ mean: how excellent is the final outcome of the abode.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 25:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification﴾ is clear, and this is revealed concerning the disbelievers. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾ means: they believe in some of the prophets and disbelieve in others. It was also said: they sever the ties of kinship (al-rahim).

His saying: ﴿and cause corruption on the earth﴾ means: they act in it with acts of disobedience. His saying: ﴿those will have the curse⁠﻿ (al-la'nah)﴾ means: distance from the mercy of Allah. His saying: ﴿and theirs will be the evil abode⁠﻿﻿⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿⁠﻿﻿ (su' al-dar)﴾ means: the evil final return, because al-munqalab (the place of return) is the people's return to the abode.

Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it for whom He wills. His saying: ﴿And they rejoice in the life of this world﴾ — al-farah (joy) is a pleasure in the heart upon attaining what one desires, and this is evidence that rejoicing in this world is prohibited and forbidden.

His saying: ﴿And the life of this world, in comparison with the Hereafter, is but a brief enjoyment﴾ — meaning: only a little. It is said: "like the provision of a rider." It is authentically related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The likeness of this world compared with the Hereafter is only like one of you dipping his finger into the sea, so let him see what it returns with."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 27:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why has a sign not been sent down upon him from his Lord?"﴾ They mean the proposed sign (al-ayah al-muqtarahah). If someone says: Why would it not be permissible for Him to grant them the proposed sign, perhaps it would be a cause of their faith? The answer: the proposed sign has no limit. If it is obligatory in the interest (al-maslahah) that He grant one, it becomes obligatory that He grant another, and so on without end.

And His saying: ﴿Say, "Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills"﴾ — its meaning is apparent. And His saying: ﴿and guides to Himself whoever turns back in repentance﴾ means: and He guides to Himself whom He wills by way of repentance (al-inabah). In the verse is a refutation of the Qadariyyah (the Qadariyyah, a early theological school who affirmed human free will in a way that denied divine predestination), and Allah is the Guide to what is correct by His favour.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 28:

And the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah.﴾ That is: their hearts become tranquil through the remembrance of Allah. It has also been said: their hearts become at ease (tasta'nis) through the remembrance of Allah. Tranquility (al-sukun) comes with certainty (al-yaqin), and agitation (al-idtirab) comes with doubt (al-shakk). Allah the Exalted said concerning the polytheists: ﴿When Allah alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter recoil.﴾ That is: they were agitated. And He said concerning the believers: ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah.﴾

As for His words: ﴿Surely in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.﴾ Its meaning: surely in the remembrance of Allah hearts become tranquil. The tranquility of the heart comes from the removal of doubt from it and the settling of certainty within it. If someone says: Did not Allah the Exalted say: ﴿Their hearts trembled﴾? So how can they tremble and find rest in one state? The answer: trembling (al-wajl) comes with the remembrance of threat and punishment, and tranquility comes with the remembrance of promise and reward. So it is as if they tremble when the justice of Allah and the severity of His reckoning are mentioned, and find rest when the bounty of Allah and His generosity are mentioned.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 29:

His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ means: and perform acts of obedience. And His statement: ﴿Blessed (ṭūbā) is for them﴾ has several interpretations. It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah, Abu Umamah and Abu al-Darda', and from Ibn 'Abbas through the narration of al-Kalbi, that they said: Ṭūbā is a tree in Paradise whose shade covers all the gardens.

In some reports, its root is in the dwelling and palace of the Prophet (ﷺ), and in every palace of Paradise there is a branch of it, and it bears every kind of fruit. Birds like the bukht (a kind of large camel) alight upon it; when the believer sees them and desires one, it falls before him, and he eats from it what he wishes, and then it flies away. And in some reports: a man who rode a swift mare or a young camel and went around its trunk would die of old age before reaching the place from which he started.

The second opinion: Ṭūbā is a name of Paradise. Mujahid said: It is the name of Paradise in Abyssinian (Ethiopic). And from 'Ikrimah: ﴿Blessed is for them﴾ means bounty for them. From Ibrahim al-Nakha'i: it means goodness and honour for them. From al-Dahhak: ﴿Blessed is for them﴾ means joy (ghibṭa) for them. The statements are close in meaning. Al-Zajjaj said: ṭūbā is on the pattern fu'lā from ṭayyib (good), and its meaning is: a good life for them.

And His statement: ﴿And a good final return﴾ means: a good place of return.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 30:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus We have sent you to a community﴾ (the verse). The meaning of the particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih) here: just as We sent the prophets to all the other nations, so We have sent you to this community.

His saying: ﴿Certainly communities have passed away before them﴾, that is: communities have already passed away before them. His saying: ﴿so that you may recite to them that which We have revealed to you﴾, that is: so that you may read to them that which We have revealed to you.

As for His saying: ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾, there are two opinions concerning it. The first: Ibn Jurayj said: the verse is Medinan, concerning the story of al-Hudaybiyya, for when Suhayl ibn 'Amr came and they agreed to write the treaty of peace, 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) wrote, "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." They said: "We do not recognize the Most Merciful. Write as we write: 'In Your name, O Allah...'" and the story continues. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾.

The second opinion, which is the well-known one: the verse is Meccan, and the occasion of its revelation was that Abu Jahl heard the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was in al-Hijr supplicating and saying: "O Allah, O Most Merciful." So he returned to the polytheists and said: "Muhammad calls upon two gods: he calls upon Allah, and he calls upon another named the Most Merciful, and we do not know the Most Merciful except the Most Merciful of al-Yamama." So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse, and He also revealed His saying: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful﴾.

As for His saying: ﴿Say: He is my Lord﴾, meaning: say, the Most Merciful is my Lord; ﴿there is no god but He; upon Him I rely, and to Him is my return﴾, meaning: upon Him I depend, in Him I trust, and to Him is repentance. Repentance (tawba) is remorse for past sins together with ceasing from them in the future.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 31:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And if only a Quran had been such that mountains were moved by it, or the earth were split asunder by it, or the dead were made to speak by it...﴾ It is related that the polytheists said to the Messenger of Allah: "Ask your Lord to move these mountains of Mecca away from us, so that our land may spread out and we may make farmland in it. Ask your Lord to bring Syria closer to us, for our trade goes there and it has become far from us." They also said: "Ask your Lord to bring forth rivers for us and to split springs in the earth, so that we may plant trees and make gardens. Ask your Lord to raise for us a group of the dead, so that we may ask them about your affair. And revive for us Qusayy, for he was a blessed old man, so that we may ask him about your affair." In some narrations they said: "Ask your Lord, by the Quran that was sent down to you, to do this." So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse: ﴿And if only a Quran had been such that mountains were moved by it...﴾ Its meaning: "And if I had decreed that I would move the mountains by a book, or cut the earth by it, or give life to the dead by it, I would have done it with this Quran."

If it is said: "This answer you give is not mentioned in the Quran, so it is an addition?"

The answer to this: the response is omitted, and the Arabs do this. The poet said:

(Had it been a single soul that died in its time... but it is a soul that falls after souls.)

Its meaning: "Had it been a single soul, I would have been consoled by it, but these are many souls." Al-Farra' mentioned that the answer is: ﴿And if only a Quran had been such that mountains were moved by it, or the earth were cut asunder by it, or the dead were made to speak by it...﴾ they would not have believed, because what preceded in our knowledge is their abandonment of faith.

Its meaning: "Even if We had done with the Quran that was sent down to you what they asked, they would still not have believed." And His words: ﴿Nay, to Allah belongs the affair entirely﴾ mean: "Nay, to Allah belongs the affair entirely in these matters; if He wills, He does them, and if He wills, He does not do them."

And His words: ﴿Have not those who believed despaired?﴾ Most of the scholars of meanings hold that its meaning is: "Have not those who believed known?" In the reading of Ibn 'Abbas it is thus: "Has it not become clear to those who believed?" This word has indeed come with the meaning of knowledge in the language of the Arabs. The poet said:

(I say to them at the ravine when they take me captive... Did you not despair that I am the son of Fares Zahdam?)

Another said:

(Did the heroes not despair that I am his son, even though I am a wanderer far from the land of my tribe?)

Al-Kisa'i denied that this bears the meaning of knowledge, and said: "The Arabs do not know despair in the sense of knowledge." He said: "The meaning of the verse is rather that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, when they heard this from the polytheists, hoped that Allah would do what they asked and that they would believe. So Allah revealed this verse: ﴿Have not those who believed despaired?﴾ meaning: despaired of the faith of these people. Whoever knows something has despaired of its opposite and its contrary." Some of them said its meaning is: "Have not those who believed known, from the condition of these unbelievers, a knowledge that necessitates their despair of their faith?" And His words: ﴿That if Allah had willed, He would have guided all mankind﴾ are clear in meaning.

And His words: ﴿And a calamity will not cease to strike those who disbelieved, for what they have done, or it will descend close to their home﴾ meaning: a disaster or affliction. It is said: the calamity here refers to the expeditions (sara'ya) of the Messenger of Allah. It is said: "or it will descend close to their home" means: the expedition will descend close to their home. It is also said: "or you yourself will descend close to their home."

﴿Until the promise of Allah comes﴾ concerning this there are two views: one is that it is the Day of Resurrection; the second view is that it is the Day of Badr.

And His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ are clear in meaning.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 32:

His saying: ﴿And indeed, messengers before you were mocked﴾. Al-istihza' (mockery): it is seeking mockery (talab al-hazl). The disbelievers used to ask these things by way of mockery, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse as consolation for the Prophet. Its meaning: "And indeed, messengers before you were mocked," that is, just as they mocked you, so messengers before you were mocked. ﴿Then I gave respite to those who disbelieved﴾: its meaning is that I granted them respite and extended the term for them. From this comes al-mulawan (the two lengthening ones), which is the night and the day. And His saying: ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My punishment?﴾: its meaning is that I seized them in this world by killing, and in the Hereafter by the Fire, so how was [My punishment] upon them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 33:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in respect of what it has earned﴾. Most of the exegetes say that His words ﴿He who stands over every soul in respect of what it has earned﴾ refer to Allah, and Allah the Exalted may not be called "qā'im" (standing) without qualification, because the Law (al-shar') did not report it, and because al-qā'im is the one who is erect (al-muntaṣib). He may, however, be described as standing in a restricted sense, namely that He stands over every soul in respect of what it has earned. The meaning of His words ﴿standing over every soul﴾ is that He is the one who takes charge of its affairs, its deeds, its provision, and other matters; and likewise He is the one who takes charge of recompense by the earning of good and evil.

Some of them said: the meaning of His words ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in respect of what it has earned﴾ is: who is knowing of the earning of every soul. The poet said:

(Had it not been for noble men of Quraysh, you would have stolen the garments of the House, and Allah is standing [watching].)

That is: knowing. His words ﴿Is then He﴾ mean: is then He who is such as this like one who does not have this attribute. His words ﴿And they have set up for Allah partners﴾ mean: they have described for Allah partners. His words ﴿Say: name them﴾ mean: describe them with the attributes that are due to them, then consider whether they are worthy of being worshipped or not.

His words ﴿Or do you inform Him of what He does not know on earth﴾ mean: or do you inform Allah of what He does not know? That is: you mention to Him a partner and another god, and He does not know of it.

His words ﴿Or with an outward saying﴾ mean: or do you hold to an outward saying that has no meaning, likened to the heedless one who does not seek the reality of the matter. It was also said: "with an outward saying" means "with a false saying." The poet said:

(The slanderers reproached me that I love her, and that complaint, its shame has become apparent [or: has departed] from you.)

That is: it has passed away. It is related that Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr recited this when he was told: "O son of the two girdles," and the speaker intended to disparage and blame him; so Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr said:

(And that complaint, its shame has become apparent from you...)

His words ﴿Nay, but their scheming has been made attractive to those who disbelieved﴾ mean: their disbelief. His words ﴿and they were barred from the way﴾ — it was also read "wa-ṣuddū" with the ṣād vowelled with a ḍammah, meaning: that was done to them. His words ﴿and they were barred﴾ mean: they themselves did that. His words ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾ — the meaning is evident.

And His saying: ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world﴾ — we have already explained the punishment in this world.

﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is harsher﴾ — meaning: more severe. And His saying: ﴿and they have no protector from Allah⁠—﴾ — meaning: no one who can shield them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 35:

And His saying: ﴿The likeness of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾. It was recited, in the irregular (shadhdh) reading: "amthāl al-Janna allatī wu'ida al-muttaqūn" (the likenesses of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised). The well-known reading is ﴿mathal al-Janna﴾ (the likeness of the Garden). Regarding it there are two opinions. The first: it is the description (ṣifa) of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised. The second opinion: the likeness of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised is a garden ﴿beneath which rivers flow; its fruit is perpetual and so is its shade﴾, meaning its fruit and its delight never cease.

If someone says: Here He said ﴿its fruit is perpetual﴾, and in another place He said ﴿and for them their provision therein, morning and evening﴾. So how is the harmony between the two verses?

The answer: permanence (dawam) means non-cessation. When it does not cease, and they are provided for morning and evening, then it is permanent. And His saying ﴿and its shade﴾ has the same meaning as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and an extended shade﴾.

In the reports: "The shade of a single tree in Paradise, a rider would travel in its shade for a hundred years without crossing it." And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is the final outcome of those who have been God-fearing﴾, its meaning: that is the final outcome of those who were God-fearing. And His saying: ﴿and the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire﴾, i.e., the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And those to whom We have given the Book rejoice at what has been revealed to you﴾ — the verse. It is narrated that the Jews who had embraced Islam used to consider the mention of al-Rahman (the Most Merciful) in the Qur'an to be little, despite its frequent mention in the Torah. So when Allah repeated the mention of al-Rahman in the Qur'an, they rejoiced, and Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse: ﴿And those to whom We have given the Book rejoice﴾ — the verse.

And His words: ﴿And among the factions are those who deny part of it﴾. The factions (al-ahzab) are those who united against the Prophet (ﷺ). His words: ﴿who deny part of it﴾ mean the mention of al-Rahman, because they did not deny the mention of Allah. His words: ﴿Say, "I have only been commanded to worship Allah and not associate anything with Him. To Him I invite, and to Him is my return."﴾ — its meaning is clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 37:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And thus We have sent it down as a judgment (ḥukman) in Arabic.﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: "an Arabic Qur'an," because it contains the rulings (al-aḥkām). The second: "an Arabic prophet," because the Prophet was from among them, and the Qur'an was revealed in their language.

And His saying: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾. Al-hawa (desire) is the inclination of the nature toward the appetite of the soul, and most of it is blameworthy. His saying: ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾, meaning: from the Qur'an. ﴿You have no protector (walī) against God, nor any defender (wāqin)﴾, meaning: no helper and no guardian.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 38:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And We had already sent messengers before you and given them wives and offspring﴾, to the end of the verse. It is related that the Jews criticised the Prophet for his having many wives, and said: "This man has no concern except for women." So God the Most High revealed this verse. It was also said: the polytheists said this, and so God the Most High revealed this verse: ﴿And We had already sent messengers before you and given them wives and offspring﴾. It is said that David had one hundred wives, and the report concerning this has been authenticated from the Prophet, and the Book also indicates it. Solomon had, according to the sound report, one thousand wives: three hundred free wives and seven hundred concubines. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿and We gave them wives and offspring﴾. Likewise, most of the prophets married and had children.

As for His words: ﴿It was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by God's leave﴾, meaning: except by God's command. ﴿For every term there is a Book﴾: its meaning is that for every term which the Shari'ah has determined, there is a Book in which it is recorded. It was also said: this is according to inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and its meaning is: for every Book there is a term and a period; and its meaning is the revealed books. It was also said: for every term there is a Book, that is, for every decree God the Most High has decreed there is a time in which it occurs, and a Book in which it is recorded.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 39:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and confirms﴾. On this there are several views. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that Allah effaces from the Shari'ah what He wills, meaning He abrogates (naskh, the abrogation of a ruling by a later one), and confirms what He wills, so it is not abrogated. It is also related from him, through the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he said: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and confirms﴾ except for wretchedness and happiness, and life and death. It is related from 'Umar and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they said: He also effaces wretchedness and happiness, and He effaces the term (ajal) and provision (rizq), and confirms what He wills. 'Umar used to say: "O Allah, if You have written me as wretched, then efface it, and write me as happy, for You have said: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and confirms﴾."

In some reports it is said that a man may have thirty years of his life remaining and then cut off his ties of kinship, so it is reduced to three days; and a man may have three days of his life remaining and then join his ties of kinship, so it is extended to thirty years.

A report supports the view of Ibn 'Abbas that wretchedness, happiness, the term and provision are not effaced. Hudhayfah ibn Usayd narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "When the drop (nutfah) settles in the womb and forty-five nights pass over it, the angel says: 'O Lord, is it male or female?' and Allah decrees, and the angel writes. Then he says: 'O Lord, is it wretched or happy?' and Allah decrees, and the angel writes. Then he says: 'O Lord, what is the term? What is the provision?' and Allah decrees, and the angel writes. Then nothing is added to it or subtracted from it." Related by Muslim in the Sahih.

There is another view on the verse, which is the view of al-Hasan: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills﴾, meaning He effaces the one whose term has arrived, and confirms the one whose term has not arrived. A fourth view on the verse is that what is meant is that the recording angels write all the deeds of the children of Adam, and Allah effaces from them what He wills, namely that which carries neither reward nor punishment, and confirms what He wills, namely that which merits reward or punishment. It was also said: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills﴾, meaning He effaces what He wills for one who disobeyed Him when his affair ends with obedience, and confirms with disobedience for one who obeyed, and his affair ends in disobedience. The views transmitted from the early generations (salaf) are those which we have mentioned before this view.

As for His words: ﴿And with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾, its meaning is: with Him is the origin of the Book, and the origin of the Book is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz). In some reports: "Allah, may He be exalted, looks into the Book that is with Him three hours before the dawn of the night; so He effaces what He wills and confirms what He wills, and changes what He wills and establishes what He wills."

And His the Exalted's saying: ﴿Whether We show you some of what We promise them﴾, the verse. "Some of what We promise them" — that is, before your death. ﴿Or We take you in death﴾ — and before We show you that. ﴿Your duty is only to convey (al-balagh)﴾ — that is, the conveying (al-tabligh). ﴿And upon Us is the reckoning﴾ on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 41:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts?﴾ Most of the exegetes hold that what is meant by this is the conquest of the lands of polytheism (shirk), and that this is called "reduction" because when the abode of Islam expands, it diminishes the abode of polytheism. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and a group of others. And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, in another narration, that he said: it is the death of the righteous and the scholars. This is also related from Mujahid. It was also said: "reducing it from its outlying parts" means by its ruin, and the Hour will arise while the whole earth is in ruins. It is said in prose sayings: "The nobles are at the edges so that the guests may come near to them." As for His words: ﴿And Allah judges; there is no repeller of His judgment﴾, meaning: there is no one who repels or diminishes His judgment. ﴿And He is swift in reckoning﴾ is clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 13, verses 42–43:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those before them had already plotted﴾. Al-makr (plotting, scheming): delivering harm to a person from a direction he does not perceive. His saying ﴿So to Allah belongs all the plotting﴾ means: with Allah is the recompense for all of their plotting. It has also been said: Allah is the creator of all of their plotting. His saying ﴿He knows what every soul earns﴾ is clear in meaning. ﴿And the disbelievers will know to whom belongs the good outcome of the abode﴾ means: whose is the final outcome of the abode. The verse is a threat and a warning. His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger"﴾ is clear in meaning. His saying ﴿Say, "Sufficient is Allah as witness"﴾ means: as a witness ﴿between me and you﴾.

His saying ﴿and [he] with whom is knowledge of the Book﴾: Qatadah said: he is Abdullah ibn Salam. It has also been said: Abdullah ibn Salam, Salman al-Farisi and Tamim al-Dari. A group of the Successors (tabi'un) also held this view. Al-Sha'bi, Ikrimah and a group of others rejected this view, and they said: the surah is Meccan, and Abdullah ibn Salam embraced Islam in Medina. Moreover, how could Allah call upon a created being as a witness? Rather, what is meant is Allah Himself. Ibn Abbas recited: "and whoever has with Him knowledge of the Book," and this makes clear that what is meant by it is Allah, Exalted is He.

It is reported that Abdullah ibn Salam himself said: I am the one meant by the verse.

It is reported from al-Hasan and Mujahid that what is meant is Allah.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is Jibril (peace be upon him). The correct view is one of the first two opinions, and Allah knows best.
